original_question: Does there exist an algorithm that efficiently converts between function values on a grid on the sphere and spherical harmonic coefficients, in both directions, with complexity roughly O(n log n) for a grid of n points?
target_in_paper: Section 5.1, "Existence of a fast discrete spherical harmonic transform," in the paper's list of open problems. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's core content almost exactly: it asks for a two-way conversion between function values sampled on a spherical grid and spherical harmonic coefficients, with a target complexity of about O(n log n) for a grid of n points. That is precisely the substance of Section 5.1. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
missing_details: The paper explicitly frames the task as the existence of a fast discrete spherical harmonic transform; naming the transform makes the question more stand-alone while staying faithful to the paper. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

The forward and inverse directions should both be stated explicitly: from sampled values on a grid on the sphere to spherical harmonic coefficients, and back again. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))

Section 5.1 itself does not specify a particular grid family, spherical-harmonic normalization, bandlimit, stability requirement, or error model, so a paper-faithful rewrite should keep those aspects neutral rather than add new assumptions. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
refined_question: Does there exist a fast discrete spherical harmonic transform; that is, an algorithm that converts function values sampled on a grid on the sphere to spherical harmonic coefficients, and also performs the inverse conversion, with complexity roughly O(n log n) for a grid of n points? ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
justification: The draft is already extremely close because the relevant target in this paper is not a theorem or conjecture with hidden algebraic hypotheses, but a short open problem stated in Section 5.1. The paper presents it as one of four open problems in orthogonal polynomials and random matrices and gives no added technical assumptions beyond the two-way transform and the desired near-linear complexity. A faithful refinement therefore only sharpens the wording by explicitly naming the discrete spherical harmonic transform and preserving the original minimal scope. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2016/071/sigma16-071.pdf))
